extracted.intended_audience: journalists, military/public information officers, and general newspaper readers
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and publishing news dispatches about wartime developments, including handling official protocols (flag display rules) and government security guidance on release of military movement information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag display precedence (U.S. flag vs U.N. flag)
rubrics_metrics.description: President Truman ordered the U.N. flag hoisted in Korea and said the U.N. flag should be displayed "concurrently with flags of various nations participating." The page notes a direct conflict: U.S. practice/Congress (1942) ruled that a flag "should be placed above or, if on the same level, to the right of the flag of the United States of America," while the U.N. (1947) ordered that "the flag of the United Nations shall not be subordinated to any other flag."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the practical and political dilemma for commanders (e.g., Gen. MacArthur) in choosing precedence. Notes likely domestic objections if the U.N. banner is placed above the U.S. flag and potential Soviet propaganda uses if U.S. flag placed second. Offers a possible solution used at U.N. headquarters: "the U.N. flag flies on top and the other flags fly in alphabetical order." Also describes the U.N. pennant's appearance (polar map enclosed in olive branches on light blue) as context for implementing display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on release of military movements and unit information (Defense Department security guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Defense Department imposed censorship-style security guidance restricting what military personnel may release about troop movements to the Korean war theatre: officers were instructed not to tell when a unit is transferring, its sailing date, its strength or its equipment; destination will be given only in general terms; nothing less than a division will be described by name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Contains the text of specific restrictions and implementation notes: 
- Continental U.S. preparations: "ultimate destination of unit alerted: refer to theater only." Numerical designation released only when unit is of division size or larger; non-divisional units to be referred to generically (e.g., "combat unit" or "supporting unit"). Status of equipment, unit strength, date of movement, and sailing time: "not releasable." "Nothing less than a division will be described by its name." 
- Naval/transport movements: Movements of naval vessels and transport/cargo ships from the West Coast may be mentioned after departure but no mention may be made of movements west of Pearl Harbor. Photographs of loadings, sailings and reactivation operations may be used within normal security limits imposed by the local commander. 
- Far East Command: "places of landing, locations and troop movements may not be disclosed until officially announced." Subordinate headquarters movements, units committed (except certain large formations such as Eighth Army, Fifth Air Force, 20th Air Force, Seventh Fleet, etc.), or any field locations may not be mentioned until officially announced. 
Also notes procedural guidance: in doubt, contact the Security Review Branch, Department of Defense (Pentagon) for advice; the rules apply only to the military giving out information and do not constitute a federal censorship law (except for atomic energy).
